newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Saudi stocks rise on foreign fund ownership news.
newsitem.headline: Saudi stocks rise on foreign fund ownership news.

text.p: Key Saudi shares clocked up good gains on Monday on news foreigners would be allowed to invest in a planned Saudi equity fund for the first time ever, dealers in the kingdom said.

Speaking by telephone from Riyadh, they said industrial giant Saudi Basic Industries Corp (SABIC) led the gains, climbing 14 riyals in the early session to 418 riyals from a 404 riyal start, and 395 on Sunday. Thirty percent of SABIC shares are traded. The rest are held by the government.

The Saudi American Bank (SAMBA), 30 percent owned by Citibank, said on Sunday it had received approval to establish what a bank official described as "a window" for foreigners to invest in Saudi stock market.

SAMBA got the go-ahead from the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency to set up the Saudi Arabian Investment Fund Ltd, which will invest exclusively in the units of SAIF KSA, which will in turn invest primarily in the shares of Saudi firms.
Shares of SAMBA, the kingdom's biggest joint venture bank, rose eight riyals on Monday to 595 riyals from 587 riyals at the start of the day. On Sunday it had closed at 586 riyals.
Riyad Bank, the second biggest bank, gained two riyals to 466 riyals.
Shares of Bank al-Jazira rose four riyals to 169 riyals.
"It is only a window for foreigners to invest in Saudi Arabian stock market through a closed-ended fund," a SAMBA official told Reuters. "The fund is open to all investors."
SAMBA officials said a team from the bank would travel to London later on Monday to discuss plans to list the fund on the London Stock Exchange.
"Subscription in the fund is expected to start in one or two months," a Riyadh-based share trader told Reuters.
The Gulf's biggest market is so far restricted to Saudis and other Gulf Arab investors. Around 70 firms are listed in the market, capitalised at around $45 billion.

Only Saudi nationals can hold shares in all local firms. Investors of the other Gulf Arab states -- Bahrain, Oman, Qatar, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates -- can own Saudi equities, excluding banks and certain other stocks.
